input:
concept: entropy
type: CONCEPT
definition: A state function measuring the number of microscopic configurations (microstates) consistent with a system's macroscopic state: S = k_B ln(Ω). Entropy quantifies unavailable energy and the direction of spontaneous change. Higher entropy means more disorder and less available work.
examples: A gas expanding into a vacuum increases entropy — more positions available to molecules | mixing two gases — more microstates than unmixed | melting ice — liquid has far more configurations than crystal
non_examples: Entropy is not simply 'disorder' in everyday sense — a living cell has low entropy but is highly organised internally
connects_to: gibbs free energy (enables), information entropy (analogous_to)
requires: second law thermodynamics, second law thermodynamics
confidence: 0.998
output: Entropy is the universe's accounting system for irreversibility. Every spontaneous process — ice melting, gas expanding, information lost — increases the total entropy of the universe. The equation S = k ln(Ω) says entropy counts the number of microscopic arrangements compatible with what you observe. More arrangements means more entropy. This is why you can never unscramble an egg.

input:
concept: boltzmann distribution
type: CONCEPT
definition: P(state s) ∝ exp(−E_s/k_BT) — the probability of a system in thermal equilibrium being in state s with energy E_s. The partition function Z = Σ exp(−E_s/k_BT) normalises the distribution. Derived by maximising entropy subject to fixed mean energy. The foundation of statistical mechanics.
examples: Atmospheric pressure decreasing with altitude — Boltzmann distribution of air molecules in gravitational potential | spin polarisation in a magnetic field: more spins align with the field at lower temperature
confidence: 0.998
output: The Boltzmann distribution tells you the probability that a system in thermal equilibrium occupies a given energy state: P(s) is proportional to exp(−E_s / k_B T). States with lower energy are exponentially more probable, and higher temperature makes high-energy states increasingly accessible. The partition function Z normalises the distribution and encodes all thermodynamic information — from it you can derive free energy, entropy, and internal energy. You can see this distribution in everyday phenomena: atmospheric pressure decreasing with altitude is just air molecules distributed in a gravitational potential according to Boltzmann's law. At the foundation of statistical mechanics, it connects microscopic physics to macroscopic thermodynamic quantities.

input:
concept: information entropy
type: CONCEPT
definition: H(X) = −Σ p(x) log2 p(x) bits. Shannon's measure of uncertainty or information content of a random variable. Maximum entropy (maximum uncertainty) when all outcomes are equally probable. Minimum entropy when one outcome has probability 1. Information gained by observing x = −log2 p(x) bits.
examples: Fair coin: H = −(0.5 log 0.5 + 0.5 log 0.5) = 1 bit | biased coin P(heads)=0.9: H = 0.469 bits | 8-sided fair die: H = 3 bits
connects_to: entropy (analogous_to)
confidence: 0.994
output: Information entropy, introduced by Claude Shannon, measures the average uncertainty in a random variable: H(X) = −Σ p(x) log₂ p(x) bits. The idea is that observing an outcome x tells you −log₂ p(x) bits of information — rare outcomes are more informative. A fair coin has 1 bit of entropy because both outcomes are equally uncertain. A biased coin with P(heads) = 0.9 has only 0.469 bits — you already knew it would likely be heads. Maximum entropy occurs when all outcomes are equally probable. Shannon's entropy is mathematically identical to Boltzmann's thermodynamic entropy, a deep connection between physics and communication theory that is not a coincidence.

input:
concept: second law thermodynamics
type: AXIOM
definition: In any spontaneous process in an isolated system, the total entropy never decreases. Heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold, never the reverse. No process is possible whose sole result is converting heat completely to work.
examples: Ice melts in warm water — entropy increases | mixing hot and cold gas — entropy increases | heat engines cannot achieve 100% efficiency
non_examples: A refrigerator appears to move heat from cold to hot, but it requires external work — total entropy including the work source still increases
connects_to: carnot cycle (enables), first law thermodynamics (precedes)
requires: entropy, entropy
confidence: 0.998
output: The second law of thermodynamics states that in any spontaneous process, the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases. This is why heat flows from hot to cold, why gas expands to fill a container, and why you can't run a heat engine at 100% efficiency. The Clausius inequality captures this mathematically: for any real process, dS ≥ δQ/T. A useful consequence is the Carnot bound — no engine operating between two reservoirs can be more efficient than the Carnot cycle. The second law is sometimes called the arrow of time because it introduces a direction to processes that the underlying equations of motion don't have.

input:
concept: gibbs free energy
type: CONCEPT
definition: G = H − TS. The Gibbs free energy determines whether a process at constant temperature and pressure is spontaneous: ΔG < 0 means spontaneous, ΔG > 0 means non-spontaneous, ΔG = 0 means equilibrium. It is the maximum non-expansion work a system can perform.
examples: ATP hydrolysis: ΔG = −30 kJ/mol — spontaneous, drives cellular processes | water boiling at 100°C and 1 atm: ΔG = 0 — liquid and vapour in equilibrium
non_examples: A reaction with ΔH < 0 (exothermic) is not necessarily spontaneous — TΔS might overcome it if T is high enough
connects_to: helmholtz free energy (similar_to)
requires: enthalpy, entropy, enthalpy, entropy
confidence: 1.000
output: Gibbs free energy G = H − TS combines enthalpy and entropy into a single criterion for spontaneity at constant temperature and pressure. A process is spontaneous when ΔG < 0, equilibrium when ΔG = 0, and non-spontaneous when ΔG > 0. It tells you the maximum non-expansion work extractable from a process — in electrochemistry, ΔG gives the electrical work a battery can deliver. At equilibrium, G is minimised, which is why reactions stop when reactants and products reach a particular ratio. The exponential relationship ΔG° = −RT ln K connects the standard free energy change directly to the equilibrium constant K.

input:
concept: carnot cycle
type: CONCEPT
definition: An idealised thermodynamic cycle operating between two heat reservoirs at temperatures T_H and T_C, consisting of two isothermal and two adiabatic processes. Its efficiency η = 1 − T_C/T_H is the maximum possible for any heat engine operating between those temperatures.
examples: A Carnot engine between 600 K and 300 K has efficiency 50% — no real engine can exceed this | Carnot efficiency increases as T_C decreases or T_H increases
non_examples: A real steam engine is not a Carnot engine — friction, irreversibility, and finite-time processes all reduce efficiency below the Carnot limit
connects_to: heat engine (enables)
requires: second law thermodynamics, reversible process, second law thermodynamics, reversible process
confidence: 0.999
output: The Carnot cycle is a theoretical thermodynamic cycle operating between two heat reservoirs at temperatures T_hot and T_cold, consisting of two isothermal and two adiabatic processes. Its efficiency η = 1 − T_cold/T_hot is the absolute maximum achievable by any heat engine — no real engine can exceed it. This isn't an engineering limitation but a consequence of the second law: extracting more work would require entropy to decrease. The Carnot cycle sets the efficiency ceiling for power stations, refrigerators, and heat pumps. In practice, irreversibilities from friction, finite temperature gradients, and non-quasi-static processes always reduce efficiency below the Carnot bound.

input:
concept: quantum superposition
type: CONCEPT
definition: A quantum system exists in a linear combination of multiple eigenstates simultaneously until measured. The state |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ is physically real — the system is genuinely in both states, not merely unknown to us. Measurement projects it to one eigenstate with probability |α|2 or |β|2.
examples: Electron spin is in superposition of | up⟩ and | down⟩ until measured
non_examples: A coin toss is NOT superposition — the coin has a definite face down, we just don't know it. Quantum superposition is physically different: the system genuinely lacks a definite value.
connects_to: quantum measurement (enables)
requires: quantum entanglement, wavefunction
confidence: 0.999
output: Quantum superposition means a system genuinely exists in multiple states simultaneously until measured. The state |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ isn't a statement about our ignorance — the system truly has no definite value for the measured property. When you measure it, the wavefunction collapses to a single eigenstate with probability |α|² or |β|². This is fundamentally different from classical uncertainty: a coin before you look is already heads or tails, you just don't know. An electron in superposition of spin-up and spin-down is neither until measured. Superposition enables quantum interference, entanglement, and the computational power of quantum computers.

input:
concept: schrodinger equation
type: AXIOM
definition: iħ ∂ψ/∂t = Ĥψ — the fundamental equation governing the time evolution of quantum wavefunctions. Ĥ is the Hamiltonian operator (total energy). The equation is linear, deterministic, and reversible. Measurement is NOT governed by the Schrödinger equation — it is governed by the Born rule.
examples: For a free particle: iħ ∂ψ/∂t = −(ħ2/2m)∇2ψ | hydrogen atom: solving with Coulomb potential gives energy levels E_n = −13.6/n2 eV
non_examples: The Dirac equation is the relativistic version — the Schrödinger equation is non-relativistic | Heisenberg's matrix mechanics is mathematically equivalent but formally different
connects_to: quantum measurement (enables), born rule (enables)
requires: wavefunction, wavefunction
confidence: 1.000
output: The Schrödinger equation iħ ∂ψ/∂t = Ĥψ governs how quantum wavefunctions evolve in time. The Hamiltonian Ĥ encodes the total energy of the system — kinetic plus potential. For stationary states, the time-independent version Ĥψ = Eψ is an eigenvalue problem: the solutions are energy eigenstates with definite energies. The equation is linear, which is why superposition holds — any linear combination of solutions is also a solution. From the hydrogen atom's discrete energy levels to quantum tunnelling, virtually all of non-relativistic quantum mechanics follows from solving the Schrödinger equation for a given potential.

input:
concept: quantum entanglement
type: CONCEPT
definition: Two or more particles in a quantum state that cannot be described independently, even when separated by arbitrary distance. Measuring one particle instantly determines the correlated state of the other. Violates Bell's inequalities, proving no local hidden variable theory can reproduce quantum predictions.
examples: Two electrons in a singlet state — measuring one as spin-up instantly makes the other spin-down regardless of separation | EPR pairs used in quantum cryptography
non_examples: Classical correlation — two gloves in separate boxes, finding one is left-handed tells you the other is right-handed — is not entanglement: the states were predetermined
connects_to: bell inequality (enables), quantum decoherence (causes)
requires: quantum superposition, quantum superposition
confidence: 0.996
output: Quantum entanglement occurs when two or more particles share a quantum state that cannot be separated into independent descriptions of each particle. Measuring one particle instantly fixes the correlated property of the other, regardless of the distance between them. This isn't faster-than-light communication — you can't control what outcome you get — but it does prove that nature is fundamentally non-local. Bell's theorem showed that no theory of local hidden variables can reproduce quantum predictions, and Bell test experiments have confirmed this. Entanglement is the resource behind quantum cryptography, quantum teleportation, and quantum computing's exponential state space.

input:
concept: quantum decoherence
type: CONCEPT
definition: The process by which a quantum system loses its coherence (ability to interfere) through entanglement with its environment. The system's reduced density matrix becomes approximately diagonal in the preferred basis — effectively classical. Decoherence does not solve the measurement problem but explains why superpositions are not observed at macroscopic scales.
examples: A large molecule in air decoheres in ~10−23 seconds — too fast to observe quantum behaviour | superconducting qubits must be cooled to milli-Kelvin to maintain coherence | Schrödinger's cat decoheres instantly
non_examples: A single atom in ultra-high vacuum can maintain coherence for seconds — decoherence is environmental, not fundamental
connects_to: quantum measurement (causes)
requires: quantum entanglement, quantum entanglement
confidence: 0.996
output: Quantum decoherence is the process by which a quantum system loses its superposition and interference properties through interaction with its environment. When a quantum system couples to environmental degrees of freedom — thermal photons, air molecules, vibrations — it becomes entangled with them. Tracing over these environmental degrees of freedom leaves the system in a classical mixture rather than a superposition. A qubit at room temperature decoheres in nanoseconds; superconducting qubits must be cooled to millikelvin to last long enough for computation. Decoherence explains why macroscopic objects appear classical — they're interacting with too many environmental particles for quantum coherence to survive.

input:
concept: wavefunction
type: CONCEPT
definition: A complex-valued function ψ(x,t) that encodes the complete quantum state of a system. The Born rule gives |ψ(x,t)|2 as the probability density of finding the particle at position x at time t. Wavefunctions must be normalised: ∫|ψ|2 dx = 1.
examples: Gaussian wavepacket for a localised particle | hydrogen 1s orbital: ψ = (1/√π)(1/a0)^(3/2) exp(−r/a0) | plane wave ψ = A exp(ikx−iωt) for a free particle
non_examples: The wavefunction is not a physical wave in 3D space — for N particles it lives in 3N-dimensional configuration space
connects_to: born rule (enables), quantum measurement (enables)
requires: schrodinger equation
confidence: 0.999
output: The wavefunction ψ(x,t) is a complex-valued mathematical object that encodes everything knowable about a quantum system. It isn't directly measurable, but its squared modulus |ψ(x,t)|² gives the probability density of finding the particle at position x. The wavefunction must be normalised — integrating |ψ|² over all space must equal 1. For a hydrogen atom's ground state, ψ decays exponentially from the nucleus, giving a probability cloud rather than a definite orbit. The wavefunction lives in configuration space: for N particles it's a function of 3N coordinates, not 3 — this is why quantum mechanics has no intuitive classical picture.

input:
concept: heisenberg uncertainty principle
type: AXIOM
definition: For any quantum system, ΔxΔp ≥ ħ/2, where Δx is the standard deviation of position, Δp of momentum, and ħ = h/2π. Similarly ΔEΔt ≥ ħ/2. These are fundamental limits — not limitations of measurement apparatus but intrinsic quantum indeterminacy.
examples: Localising an electron to Δx = 1 Å forces Δp ≥ 5.3×10−25 kg·m/s — enormous momentum uncertainty | virtual particles exist for time Δt ≤ ħ/(2ΔE) permitted by energy uncertainty
non_examples: Observer effect in photography — disturbing the object — is NOT the uncertainty principle. HUP holds even with ideal, non-disturbing measurements.
connects_to: quantum measurement (enables)
requires: quantum superposition, wavefunction
confidence: 0.998
output: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle states that position and momentum cannot both be known precisely simultaneously: ΔxΔp ≥ ħ/2. This isn't a limitation of our instruments — it's an intrinsic feature of quantum reality. A particle described by a narrow wavepacket is well-localised in space but its momentum is spread over many values, and vice versa. Confine an electron to a 1Å box and it gains enormous momentum uncertainty, which is why electrons don't fall into atomic nuclei. The energy-time relation ΔEΔt ≥ ħ/2 permits virtual particles to briefly violate energy conservation, underpinning quantum field theory phenomena like the Casimir effect.

input:
concept: overfitting
type: CONCEPT
definition: A model learns the training data too well — including its noise and idiosyncrasies — and fails to generalise to new data. Occurs when model capacity is high relative to training data volume. Evidenced by low training loss with high validation loss. The central challenge of ML with small datasets.
examples: A polynomial of degree 99 fitting 100 training points perfectly but oscillating wildly — 0 training error, terrible generalisation | Flux's LTC with 128-dim hidden state trained on 112 sessions risks overfitting
non_examples: High bias (underfitting) — model is too simple to capture the patterns — is the opposite problem
confidence: 0.973
output: Overfitting occurs when a model learns the training data too well — including its noise and random fluctuations — and loses the ability to generalise to new examples. The tell-tale sign is a large gap between training loss and validation loss: the model is memorising rather than learning structure. It happens when model capacity is high relative to the amount of training data. A degree-99 polynomial can fit 100 training points perfectly but oscillates wildly between them, producing terrible predictions elsewhere. Solutions include regularisation (constraining the model), dropout, early stopping, and collecting more data. Overfitting is the central challenge of machine learning with small or noisy datasets.

input:
concept: gradient descent
type: ACTION
definition: An iterative optimisation algorithm: θ_{t+1} = θ_t − η∇L(θ_t). Parameters θ are updated by subtracting the gradient of the loss L scaled by learning rate η. The gradient points uphill; descending it minimises the loss. Convergence depends on η, loss landscape geometry, and initialisation.
examples: Training a neural network: compute loss → backprop → update all weights | stochastic GD: use one sample per step — noisy but fast | mini-batch: compromise between batch accuracy and speed
non_examples: Second-order methods (Newton, L-BFGS) that use the Hessian are not gradient descent — they use curvature information
requires: gradient vector
confidence: 0.993
output: Gradient descent is the algorithm that teaches neural networks by repeatedly nudging every weight in the direction that reduces loss. At each step you compute the gradient of the loss with respect to all parameters, then subtract a small fraction of it — the learning rate times the gradient. Do this enough times and the network converges to a minimum.

input:
concept: backpropagation
type: ACTION
definition: Efficient computation of gradients in neural networks via the chain rule applied backward through the computational graph. Forward pass: compute loss. Backward pass: propagate ∂L/∂output backward, computing ∂L/∂parameter for every parameter using cached intermediate values. Time complexity same as forward pass.
examples: Loss → ∂L/∂output → ∂L/∂W_last → ... → ∂L/∂W_first, all in one backward pass | automatic differentiation (autograd) implements backprop for arbitrary computations
requires: chain rule, gradient descent
confidence: 0.986
output: Backpropagation is just the chain rule applied backwards through a computational graph. You run the forward pass, compute loss, then walk back through every operation reversing it — multiplying partial derivatives as you go. What comes out is the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight in the network. Gradient descent then uses those gradients to nudge each weight. Without backprop, training deep networks would require finite differences, which is 10,000× slower.

input:
concept: transformer architecture
type: AI_SYSTEM
definition: A neural architecture based entirely on attention mechanisms, without recurrence. Encoder-decoder or decoder-only variants. Key components: multi-head self-attention, position-wise feedforward layers, layer normalisation, residual connections, and positional encoding (since attention is permutation-invariant).
examples: GPT series: decoder-only transformer | BERT: encoder-only | T5: encoder-decoder
non_examples: LSTMs and GRUs process sequences recurrently — they are not Transformers
requires: attention mechanism
confidence: 0.991
output: The Transformer is a neural network architecture built entirely on attention mechanisms, without recurrence or convolutions. Every position in the input sequence attends to every other position simultaneously — this is self-attention. A Transformer has an encoder (bidirectional attention) and a decoder (causal, autoregressive attention with cross-attention to the encoder). Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel, each attending to different aspects of the sequence. The architecture parallelises completely over sequence length, which makes it far more trainable than LSTMs on modern GPUs. GPT uses decoder-only Transformers; BERT uses encoder-only; T5 uses the full encoder-decoder stack.

input:
concept: attention mechanism
type: CONCEPT
definition: A function that computes a weighted sum of values where weights are determined by the similarity between queries and keys: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T/√d_k)V. Allows every position to attend to every other — captures long-range dependencies. The core of Transformers.
examples: In machine translation, the decoder attends to encoder positions most relevant to the current output word | self-attention: queries, keys, values all come from the same sequence
requires: softmax function
confidence: 0.998
output: The attention mechanism computes a weighted sum of values, where the weights come from comparing a query against a set of keys: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T/√d_k)V. High similarity between a query and a key means the corresponding value gets a large weight. Scaled dot-product attention divides by √d_k to prevent the dot products from growing large in high dimensions, which would push softmax into near-zero gradient regions. In self-attention, queries, keys, and values all come from the same sequence, so every token can attend to every other token. This gives the model global context with no fixed receptive field, which is why Transformers handle long-range dependencies far better than RNNs.

input:
concept: regularization
type: ACTION
definition: Techniques to reduce overfitting by constraining model complexity or adding noise. L2 (weight decay): adds λ||w||2 to loss — penalises large weights. L1: adds λ|w| — induces sparsity. Dropout: randomly zeroes neurons during training. Early stopping: halts training when validation loss stops improving.
examples: AdamW uses weight_decay=0.01 — adds L2 penalty to all weights | Dropout(0.1) in Flux's LTC cell — 10% of hidden units zeroed each step during training
confidence: 0.983
output: Regularisation is the set of techniques used to prevent overfitting by constraining model complexity. L2 regularisation adds λ||w||² to the loss, penalising large weights and shrinking parameters toward zero — this is weight decay in AdamW. L1 regularisation adds λ|w|, which drives some weights exactly to zero, producing sparse models. Dropout randomly zeroes a fraction of neurons during each training step, preventing units from co-adapting and acting as implicit ensemble training. Early stopping monitors validation loss and halts training when it stops improving, preventing the model from memorising training noise. All of these methods reduce effective model capacity without changing the architecture.

input:
concept: thermodynamic equilibrium
type: CONCEPT
definition: A state in which a system's macroscopic properties (temperature, pressure, volume, composition) are uniform throughout and constant in time with no net flows of energy or matter. Requires simultaneous mechanical, thermal, and chemical equilibrium.
examples: Gas in a sealed insulated container left long enough — uniform T, P | water and ice at 0°C in an insulated container at the melting point
non_examples: A rod with one end in fire — temperature gradient exists, not in equilibrium | a living cell — maintains non-equilibrium by consuming energy
connects_to: entropy (enables)
requires: zeroth law thermodynamics
confidence: 0.999
output: Thermodynamic equilibrium is the state a system reaches when all macroscopic properties — temperature, pressure, volume, chemical composition — are uniform throughout and constant in time, with no net flows of energy or matter. It requires mechanical equilibrium (no pressure gradients), thermal equilibrium (uniform temperature), and chemical equilibrium (no net reactions). A gas in a sealed insulated container reaches equilibrium; a living cell never does — it maintains non-equilibrium by constantly consuming energy. The zeroth law of thermodynamics establishes that thermal equilibrium is transitive: if A is in equilibrium with B and B with C, then A and C are in equilibrium, which is what makes temperature a well-defined, measurable quantity.

input:
concept: partition function
type: CONCEPT
definition: Z = Σ_s exp(−βE_s) where β = 1/k_BT. All thermodynamic quantities follow from Z: F = −k_BT ln Z (Helmholtz free energy), U = −∂ ln Z/∂β (internal energy), S = k_B(ln Z + βU) (entropy). The partition function encodes the entire thermodynamic content of a statistical mechanical model.
examples: Two-level system: Z = 1 + exp(−βε) | ideal gas: Z = (2πmk_BT/h2)^{3N/2} V^N/N! | quantum harmonic oscillator: Z = 1/(1 − exp(−βħω))
requires: boltzmann distribution
confidence: 0.997
output: The partition function Z = Σ_s exp(−βE_s) is the central object of statistical mechanics, where β = 1/k_BT. It's a sum over all microstates weighted by their Boltzmann factors. The key insight is that all thermodynamic properties follow from Z by differentiation: the Helmholtz free energy F = −k_BT ln Z, the internal energy U = −∂ ln Z/∂β, and entropy S = k_B(ln Z + βU). Once you know Z, you know everything about the system at equilibrium. For a two-level system it's Z = 1 + exp(−βε); for an ideal gas it becomes a product over all N particles; for the quantum harmonic oscillator it yields a geometric series.

input:
concept: first law thermodynamics
type: AXIOM
definition: The total energy of an isolated system is conserved: ΔU = Q − W, where ΔU is the change in internal energy, Q is heat added to the system, and W is work done by the system. Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed.
examples: A gas heated in a piston absorbs Q joules, does W joules of work expanding, and its internal energy rises by Q−W | burning fuel converts chemical energy to heat and mechanical work
non_examples: A perpetual motion machine of the first kind — producing work with no energy input — violates this law
connects_to: zeroth law thermodynamics (precedes), second law thermodynamics (precedes)
requires: internal energy, internal energy, heat, thermodynamic work
confidence: 1.000
output: The first law of thermodynamics states that energy is conserved: the change in internal energy equals heat added to the system minus work done by the system, ΔU = Q − W. It rules out perpetual motion machines of the first kind — you cannot create energy from nothing. When a gas in a piston absorbs heat Q and expands doing work W, its internal energy rises by exactly Q − W. The first law is agnostic about the direction of processes — it says energy is conserved whether heat flows from hot to cold or cold to hot. That directionality is the job of the second law. Together, the first and second laws are the two pillars of classical thermodynamics.

input:
concept: helmholtz free energy
type: CONCEPT
definition: A = U − TS. The Helmholtz free energy gives the maximum work extractable from a system at constant temperature and volume: ΔA = W_max. At equilibrium, A is minimised. Useful for systems at constant T and V — common in statistical mechanics.
examples: Battery at constant temperature delivers work up to | ΔA | statistical mechanics often minimises A to find equilibrium
connects_to: gibbs free energy (similar_to)
requires: entropy, internal energy, entropy
confidence: 1.000
output: The Helmholtz free energy A = U − TS gives the maximum work extractable from a system at constant temperature and volume. When a system can exchange heat with a reservoir at temperature T, the free energy available for useful work is the total energy U reduced by the unavailable portion TS — the entropy tax. At equilibrium, A is minimised, which is why spontaneous processes at constant T and V always decrease A. In statistical mechanics, A = −k_BT ln Z, connecting the partition function directly to the free energy. For most laboratory settings where pressure rather than volume is held constant, the Gibbs free energy G = H − TS is more useful, but in statistical mechanics and condensed matter, Helmholtz is the natural choice.

input:
concept: canonical ensemble
type: CONCEPT
definition: Statistical description of a system in thermal contact with a heat bath at temperature T, with fixed V and N but fluctuating energy. Energy follows the Boltzmann distribution. This is the most practically useful ensemble — most lab experiments are at controlled temperature.
requires: boltzmann distribution, partition function
confidence: 0.950
output: The canonical ensemble describes a system in thermal contact with a heat bath at fixed temperature T, with fixed particle number N and volume V, but with energy that fluctuates. It is the most practically useful statistical ensemble because most real experiments are performed at controlled temperature rather than controlled energy. The probability of the system being in a microstate with energy E_s is the Boltzmann distribution P(s) = exp(−βE_s)/Z. The canonical ensemble connects microscopic physics to macroscopic thermodynamics through the partition function Z, from which all equilibrium properties can be derived. It sits between the microcanonical ensemble (fixed energy) and the grand canonical ensemble (fixed chemical potential with fluctuating particle number).

input:
concept: flux ltc model
type: AI_SYSTEM
definition: Flux's Liquid Time-Constant neural network — a continuous-time recurrent model that processes [TEACH] sessions character by character and produces a hidden state summarising the session. The hidden state drives the consolidation head (trust decision) and spec head (formal language prediction).
examples: 82-token character vocabulary | embed_dim=32 | hidden_dim=128
confidence: 0.993
output: Flux's LTC model is a Liquid Time-Constant recurrent neural network — a continuous-time model that processes teaching sessions character by character. Unlike standard RNNs that update at discrete steps, LTC neurons have time constants that adapt based on the input, giving the model a form of temporal self-regulation. The hidden state produced after reading a full session condenses everything Flux learned from that session into a 128-dimensional vector. This vector then feeds two heads: the consolidation head, which decides whether to trust and integrate the new knowledge, and the spec head, which predicts formal language patterns. The LTC's strength is sequential processing of character streams with temporal dynamics — it is not designed for semantic discrimination or text generation.

input:
concept: neural plasticity
type: CONCEPT
definition: The brain's ability to reorganise its structure and function in response to experience, learning, injury, or development. Occurs at multiple scales: synaptic (LTP/LTD), dendritic (spine growth), axonal (sprouting), and cortical map reorganisation. 'Use it or lose it' — unused connections weaken.
examples: London taxi drivers have larger hippocampal posterior regions after years of spatial navigation | phantom limb pain — cortical remapping after amputation | stroke recovery — adjacent regions take over lost functions
confidence: 0.950
output: Neural plasticity is the brain's ability to reorganise its structure and connections in response to experience, learning, and injury. It operates at multiple scales: at the synapse, long-term potentiation strengthens frequently co-activated connections while long-term depression weakens rarely used ones — Hebb's rule in biological form. At larger scales, the cortical map itself can reorganise: London taxi drivers develop larger hippocampal posterior regions from years of spatial navigation, and after amputation, adjacent cortical regions expand into the territory of the lost limb, producing phantom sensations. The principle 'use it or lose it' governs plasticity throughout the lifespan — critical periods early in development have heightened plasticity, while adult plasticity, though reduced, never fully disappears.

input:
concept: cross entropy loss
type: CONCEPT
definition: L = −Σi yi log(ŷi). For a one-hot true distribution, reduces to −log(ŷ_{true class}). Measures how many bits are needed to encode the true distribution using the model's predicted distribution. Minimising cross-entropy is equivalent to maximising log-likelihood.
examples: Language model training: cross-entropy over next token | Flux's spec_head language prediction: cross_entropy(lang_logits, true_lang_index)
requires: softmax function, loss function
confidence: 0.998
output: Cross-entropy loss measures how many bits the model's predicted distribution wastes compared to the true distribution: L = −Σ y_i log(ŷ_i). For a classification task with one-hot labels, this reduces to −log(ŷ_{true class}) — the negative log-probability the model assigned to the correct answer. A model that assigns the correct class probability 0.01 incurs a loss of 6.6; one that assigns 0.99 incurs 0.01. Minimising cross-entropy is equivalent to maximising log-likelihood, which is equivalent to minimising KL divergence from the true distribution. In language modelling, cross-entropy over next-token prediction is the standard training objective — perplexity, the standard language model evaluation metric, is simply 2 raised to the cross-entropy.

input:
concept: transfer learning
type: ACTION
definition: Using knowledge (parameters) learned in one task or domain as the starting point for a new task. Fine-tuning a pretrained model on domain-specific data. The pretrained representations encode general structure (e.g., language syntax) that is expensive to learn from scratch but transfers cheaply.
examples: Fine-tuning Whisper for a specific accent on 100 examples | starting from a pretrained LLM for LUMEN rather than training from scratch | Flux's embedding layer — trained from scratch (too small to transfer from), but expand_vocab() preserves learned embeddings when vocab grows
confidence: 0.978
output: Transfer learning means starting a new task from parameters already trained on a related task, rather than from random initialisation. Pretrained models have already learned general representations — syntax, visual edges, physical dynamics — that are expensive to learn from scratch and transfer cheaply. Fine-tuning a pretrained language model on a domain-specific dataset requires orders of magnitude less data than training from scratch. The intuition is that early layers learn universal features and later layers learn task-specific ones, so you fine-tune the later layers more aggressively while keeping the early layers nearly frozen. The alternative, training from scratch, is sometimes necessary when the source and target domains are too dissimilar for the pretrained representations to help.

input:
concept: eigenstate
type: CONCEPT
definition: a quantum state that is a definite eigenvalue state of an observable operator. If operator O acts on state |psi> and returns O|psi> = lambda|psi>, then |psi> is an eigenstate of O with eigenvalue lambda. Measurement of O on an eigenstate always yields lambda with certainty.
examples: the energy eigenstates of the hydrogen atom are | n,l,m> with eigenvalues E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV | a spin-up state
non_examples: a superposition of energy eigenstates is NOT an eigenstate of the Hamiltonian | a coherent state of the harmonic oscillator is not an energy eigenstate
connects_to: wave function collapse (enables)
requires: superposition, hamiltonian, wavefunction, quantum measurement
confidence: 0.987
output: An eigenstate of an observable operator O is a quantum state that, when acted on by O, returns a scalar multiple of itself: O|ψ⟩ = λ|ψ⟩. The scalar λ is the eigenvalue — the definite value you will measure for that observable with certainty. Energy eigenstates of the hydrogen atom form the familiar orbital shapes with energies E_n = −13.6/n² eV. A particle in an energy eigenstate has no energy uncertainty: every measurement returns exactly E_n. In contrast, a superposition of energy eigenstates has energy uncertainty — each measurement can return any of the component eigenvalues with probability given by the squared amplitude. Measurement always projects the quantum state onto an eigenstate of the measured observable.

input:
concept: superposition
type: CONCEPT
definition: a quantum system exists simultaneously in multiple distinct states until measured. The state is a linear combination of basis states: psi = sum_i c_i |i>, where c_i are complex amplitudes and |c_i|^2 is the probability of outcome i. Superposition is destroyed by measurement, which collapses the state to a single eigenstate.
examples: a qubit in state ( | 0> + | 1>)/sqrt(2) has equal probability of being 0 or 1 on measurement
non_examples: a classical coin that is heads or tails but unknown — that is classical probability, not superposition | a random variable drawn from a probability distribution
connects_to: wave function collapse (enables), entanglement (enables), interference (enables)
requires: schrodinger equation, wavefunction, quantum measurement
confidence: 0.993
output: Quantum superposition means a system exists in a linear combination of distinct quantum states simultaneously: |ψ⟩ = Σ c_i|i⟩. The complex amplitudes c_i determine the probabilities — |c_i|² is the probability of finding the system in state |i⟩ on measurement. Before measurement, the system genuinely has no definite value for the observable — it inhabits all possibilities at once. This is what makes superposition different from classical probability: a coin in a box is definitely heads or tails but unknown to you; an electron in spin superposition is neither spin-up nor spin-down until the measurement itself creates the outcome. Superposition is destroyed by measurement, by decoherence from environmental interaction, and it is the resource that makes quantum interference and entanglement possible.

input:
concept: decoherence
type: CONCEPT
definition: the process by which a quantum system loses its superposition and phase coherence through interaction with an environment. The system becomes entangled with environmental degrees of freedom, and tracing over the environment yields a diagonal density matrix — destroying quantum interference. Decoherence explains why macroscopic objects appear classical.
examples: a qubit coupled to thermal photons loses coherence in nanoseconds | superconducting qubits must be cooled to millikelvin to slow decoherence | Schrodinger cat states decohere faster for larger systems
non_examples: wave function collapse due to measurement is separate from decoherence | energy dissipation (friction) is classical decoherence's classical analogue but not identical
connects_to: wave function collapse (enables), quantum measurement (enables)
requires: density matrix, density matrix, superposition, entanglement
confidence: 0.997
output: Decoherence is the process by which quantum superpositions are destroyed through interaction with the environment. When a quantum system couples to external degrees of freedom — thermal photons, air molecules, vibrations — it becomes entangled with them. Once entangled with the environment, tracing over the environmental degrees of freedom leaves the system in a statistical mixture rather than a coherent superposition, destroying quantum interference. Decoherence happens faster for larger, more complex systems: a single electron can maintain coherence for microseconds in isolation, while macroscopic objects decohere in femtoseconds. This is why we never see cats in superposition — the interaction rate with the surrounding environment is enormous. Quantum computers must operate at millikelvin temperatures to slow decoherence enough for useful computation.

input:
concept: dark matter
type: CONCEPT
definition: Non-luminous matter that interacts gravitationally but not electromagnetically, hypothesised to explain galaxy rotation curves, gravitational lensing, and large-scale structure formation. Constitutes ~27% of the universe's energy content. The specific particle has not been detected despite many experiments.
examples: Galaxy rotation curves are flat where they should decrease — implying unseen mass | Bullet Cluster: dark matter (gravitational lensing) and visible gas (X-ray) separated in a galactic collision
confidence: 0.974
output: Dark matter is the name physicists give to whatever is making galaxies rotate too fast. We can see its gravitational effects everywhere — it bends light, holds galaxy clusters together — but it emits no light of its own and has never been directly detected. It makes up about 27% of the universe's mass-energy. The leading candidates are WIMPs and axions, but nothing is confirmed yet.
